title: The “bottom-line” associations: a scientific saga
bodyHtml:
With great power comes great polygenicity!

Arc 1: Introduction


It’s been almost two centuries since Gregor Mendel gifted the world with his stories about the humble peas, and almost two decades since the first major genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of seven common diseases were published1. Despite certain doubts about their utility, it is undeniable that GWAS provide valuable first clues in our search for disease culprits, as showcased by the guilty verdicts of NOD2 in Crohn’s disease2 and TCF7L2 in type 2 diabetes3. Motivated by these successes, within 20 years, we have produced >100,000 GWAS for thousands of diseases and complex traits4. No longer the scarcity of genetic data, we are now, however, confronted by its abundance: with so many GWAS for each trait (sometimes producing conflicting results), which one should we trust to draw conclusions from or to follow up in subsequent analyses?

The default answer for many is to choose the largest and latest GWAS, often regarded as the most comprehensive study. This assumption falls short when the largest GWAS does not subsume every smaller study or when it removes variants of lower sample sizes. As a result, we may fail to detect certain true associations. The second default is to simply check whether an association is significant in any GWAS, ignoring the rest where it fails to replicate. Unless it’s peak summertime in the Pacific Northwest, cherry-picking shouldn’t be any scientist’s favorite activity! Not only statistically invalid but this approach also cannot produce a coherent set of summary results for any follow-up analysis that requires genome-wide statistics. The ideal solution then is to pool together the genotype of participants across all cohorts for a meta-analysis – but ideal is never realistic – this process is very costly, if at all possible.

Fortunately, just like how the lack of raw talent can be overcome with persistent effort, we don’t need raw genotype data to create the ‘GOAT’ of GWAS. Nor should we try to – it probably doesn’t exist. To resolve the GWAS ‘paradox of choice’, our team at the Knowledge Portal Network and colleagues from the University of Michigan have developed the ‘bottom-line’ procedure that meta-analyzes summary statistics from published GWAS. We apply this procedure on a large scale to generate one bottom-line association statistic for each variant for each of ~1,300 complex traits and diseases. In our manuscript5, we show that the bottom-line associations balance between comprehensiveness (not guaranteed by the largest GWAS) and precision (a drawback of using any GWAS), and produce reliable downstream results.

 

Arc 2: Invitation


So, if you are a computational biologist overwhelmed by GWAS resources, a bench scientist seeing conflicting GWAS signals for your experimental targets, or a strong advocate for reproducibility in science, you are in the right place! We invite you to explore the bottom-line associations and brainstorm on how they may or may not be relevant to your research. You can access these associations in three ways.

If you would like to bulk-download the bottom-line summary statistics, for each phenotype ID ‘p’ and ancestry ID ‘a’, you can use the following command: ‘aws s3 --no-sign-request cp s3://dig-open-bottom-line-analysis/bottom-line/$a/$p.sumstats.tsv.gz $download_location’. The full lists of phenotypes and ancestries are available here.

If you’ve drank too much coffee and are now feeling ‘gittery’, check out our Github repository. The functions in this repo allow you to explore the bottom-line results without downloading them.

If you are curious about how the bottom-line results are used in downstream analyses, you can search for a phenotype of interest on the Home page of the A2FKP to go to its Phenotype page. On the Phenotype page (for example, heart failure), you can manually download the summary statistics (Fig. 1A). Further down, we show the number of potentially novel bottom-line signals (Fig. 1B) and the datasets that contributed to the bottom-line statistics (Fig. 1C). Lingering a little longer, you will also see the prioritized genes, pathways, tissues, and many more insights about your phenotype. Many results on this page are linked to others on the A2FKP so you can choose your own adventure!

 

Arc 3: Tribute

 

Contrary to what the name may suggest, the bottom-line associations are not our end goal but rather, just the start of our quest for disease causes and mechanisms. In almost every page and tool on the A2FKP, the essence of the bottom-line seeps into each visualization and analysis. Gene-level associations on the Gene page? The PheWAS plot on the Variant page? Global enrichment of functional annotations across tissues on the Phenotype page? They are all derivatives of the bottom-line. And we’re giving them all back! To you. Our dear users. Our expert collaborators. Most importantly, our contributors who have entrusted us with your data. So thank you! Our door is always open if you ever drop by to offer a basket of research results, take a tour around the portal, or simply chat about science.

I’d like to end the blog in the first-person voice here. Over the past five years of incorporating hundreds of GWAS into the bottom-line analysis and working on the manuscript, I’ve always held one word close to my heart: stewardship. We are not just data analysts who crunch the numbers, or software developers who build browsers and apps, or project managers who hold teams together. We are stewards of our community garden, collecting seeds from everyone, watering them with care and thought, and sending the wonderful produce back. Science is hard. Not every season is fruitful. But seeing our work show up in others’ makes it all worth it. And I hope that one day, those tiny colorful dots on each Manhattan plot, much like Mendel’s beloved peas, will realize what a significant place they hold amid the chamber of history.

 

Written by Trang Nguyen, Computational Biologist at the KPN

 

References
